prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

The plate is headed "acrylic", with the standing line "A painter's desktop app that turns a reference image into real acrylic paints, mixing recipes, and a shopping list." beneath it.

The dominant picture, filling roughly half the page, shows A photograph lies on the table at left. From it, ten swatch chips lift away in a descending line, largest first. Each chip travels right toward a fanned shelf of paint tubes, the catalog. Beside each chip, three candidate tubes stand in ranked order. A mixing bar shows a proportioned blend of two tubes whose result sits next to the original chip for comparison. One arrow runs from photograph to chips to tubes to recipe.

Magnified circles set beside it show The first circle shows image pixels gathering into a few colour clusters. The second shows a measuring ruler between the target chip and a paint swatch, marked in ΔE bands. The third shows a mixing bar split two parts to three. In the studies, a paint tube carries a checkmark toggle for ownership. A two-position switch chooses between the whole catalog and your own tubes.

Colour is used so that Cadmium red marks paints you still need to buy. Ultramarine marks measurement and ΔE distance. Warm ochre marks the colour extracted from the image.

Draw these quantities as dimension marks or counts: 117 Golden Acrylics in the catalog. 2 to 40 colors, default 10. Top 3 single-paint matches per colour. Mixing ratios from 1:9 to 9:1. ΔE bands below 1, 2, 5, and 10. Image resized to at most 256 by 256. 4 PDF exports.

These trade words appear on the plate, each set against the thing it names: K-Means++ sits on the clustering circle. CIEDE2000 and ΔE sit on the measuring ruler. Perfect, Excellent, Good, and Approximate sit on the ruler bands. Mixing Recipe sits on the blend bar. Best Match and From My Collection sit on the switch. Owned and Need sit on the tube toggle. Comparison, Color Detail, Shopping List, and Paint by Numbers sit on the exported pages. acrylic.db sits on the database drum, state.json on the settings file, and projects on the image folder.

Letter these words onto the drawings, spelled exactly as given: Reference image, Dominant colors, Pixel count, Paint catalog, Top 3 matches, Mixing Recipe. K-Means++, CIEDE2000, Perfect, Excellent, Good, Approximate. Best Match, From My Collection, Owned, Need. Comparison, Color Detail, Shopping List, Paint by Numbers. acrylic.db, state.json, projects.

Set these short notes beside what they explain: Image shrunk before clustering for speed; Dominant first, ranked by pixel count. Perceptual distance, not raw screen difference; Two paints tried first, then three. Owned paints drop off the list. Lists only paints you do not own; Paint-by-numbers export is still a placeholder. Changing a setting rebuilds the palette.
